title: Keeping a commonplace book: saving sentences that save you
description: For centuries, readers have copied out the sentences they wanted to keep into a single notebook — a commonplace book. It is not a diary and not a journal. It is a treasury of other people's best lines, gathered for your future self.

body.heading: What goes in
paragraphs: Anything that makes you stop and reread: a line from a novel, a sentence from a letter, a proverb your grandmother uses, a fragment of a speech. Copy it by hand if you can — the slowness is part of the point, because a sentence you have written out is a sentence you have actually read twice.
Add the source and, when it matters, a few words about why it struck you. “For the week of the move” beside a line about patience will mean more in five years than the line alone.

body.heading: Why it works
paragraphs: A commonplace book quietly builds a portrait of your taste. Rereading it after a year shows you what you were hungry for — courage, calm, wit, consolation — often before you knew you were looking.

It also gives you company on demand. On a flat or difficult day, ten minutes with sentences you once chose is a conversation with every writer who ever steadied you, plus the past self who did the choosing.

body.heading: Start embarrassingly small
paragraphs: One notebook, one line a week. Do not organise it, index it, or decorate it unless decorating is the pleasure. The only rule is that the line must have earned its place by moving you.
Within a few months you will own a small, strange, personal anthology that no shop sells: the book of sentences your life has been collecting on purpose.

takeaway: Copy out the sentences that stop you, note why they mattered, and you build a treasury your future self will thank you for.
